name: Lina Colucci
bio: Co-Founder and CEO of LemonSlice, an AI lab working to break the avatar Turing test. LemonSlice raised $10.5M seed from Matrix and YC and have the most advanced interactive avatar model in the world. Originally from Brazil, Lina is an ML researcher and artist - ballerina, musician, photographer, YouTuber. She previously founded and ran one of the leading ML consulting firms in the US, and has a PhD from MIT and Harvard.

positions.claim: Turn taking is an audio engineering problem, not an LLM problem — a perfect model with a bad audio pipeline still produces a broken experience.
Humans switch conversational turns in about 200ms; agent response feels off at 800ms and users abandon at 1.5 seconds.
755ms is the best measured voice-to-voice response time for a cascaded pipeline, roughly 4x slower than human turn taking.
There is no universally correct minimum-silence threshold; the right value depends on domain, around 200ms for a sales agent and 1000-1200ms where users need thinking time.
VAD alone cannot distinguish a completed sentence, an incomplete thought, a thinking pause, and a backchannel acknowledgement because the silence signal is identical.
STT-provider turn detection makes better decisions than VAD because it uses full audio plus linguistic context, but costs you observability into why it fired.
Smart Turn v3.2's 58.9% recall is acceptable in production because a VAD timer runs underneath as a safety net, so misses only cost latency, not correctness.
Smart Turn v3.2 at 58.9% recall is the best deployable turn detection available today, since higher-recall research results like Meta's 87.7% have no released code.
A standard cloud-API voice pipeline totals roughly 1,100-1,300ms, with LLM time to first byte at 500-650ms as the dominant component.
Co-locating all models in one GPU cluster gets total voice-to-voice down to about 500ms, making that the achievable floor for teams willing to invest in infrastructure.
STT and LLM together consume about two-thirds of the latency budget and are therefore the only two meaningful levers for improving it.
P95 latency matters more than P50 for voice agents because a single slow response destroys the conversation and cannot be averaged away.
LLMs should be held to a sub-700ms time-to-first-token target for voice applications.
Instruction following degrades after roughly 15-20 turns, requiring context pruning or session resets in long voice conversations.
False interruptions measurably increase escalation rates to human agents.
Agents should not stop for every detected interruption — corrections warrant stopping while backchannels and background noise do not.
The three levels are configuration choices, not architectural ones — the Pipecat pipeline code is essentially identical across all three.
Production systems should combine a turn detection model with silence detection rather than relying on either alone.
Owning the turn detection stack locally is worth it when you need compliance control or want to fine-tune on your own data.
